Studies on the Yellow-chinned Anole (Anolis gundlachi) have documented key morphological traits that define its life history. Hatchlings emerge from eggs with a snout-vent length (SVL) of 1.5 cm [Lb = 1.5 cm], a diminutive size that renders them vulnerable to predation. Remarkably, field observations have occasionally recorded hatchling A. gundlachi individuals recovered from the stomach contents of coqui frogs, underscoring the intense predation pressure faced by neonates in the Puerto Rican forest floor leaf litter. This small initial body size is accompanied by a correspondingly low wet weight at birth, calculated from allometric scaling relationships for the species as approximately 0.12 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.12 grams]. Such a modest neonatal mass likely reflects the constrained energy budget of egg production in this insectivorous lizard and necessitates a rapid initial growth phase to escape the size window of high vulnerability.

Embryonic development in Anolis gundlachi, monitored under controlled conditions at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is completed in an average of 43 days [ab = 43 days]. This incubation length is somewhat prolonged compared to some lowland congeners and likely reflects the cooler montane microhabitats this species occupies. The resulting hatchling, a yolk-sac larva equipped with internalized yolk reserves, is fully reliant on its endogenous energy stores for the first few days post-hatching before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The embryonic development temperature exerts a strong influence on the duration of this phase, with even minor thermal fluctuations leading to noticeable shifts in hatching timing, an important consideration given the thermal variability of the shaded microsites where females deposit their eggs.

As juveniles grow, they undergo a period of rapid mass gain before transitioning into the sub-adult stage. Sexual maturation, defined by the onset of gonadal activation, is typically attained at a snout-vent length of 4 cm [Lp = 4 cm]. At this pubertal milestone, the estimated wet weight of an individual is approximately 1.54 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.54 grams], derived from the same length-mass relationship used for neonates. This size at puberty represents a substantial multiple of the hatchling mass, reflecting the successful accumulation of somatic tissue during the juvenile phase. The attainment of this size is not merely a matter of age but is strongly contingent on local resource availability, with individuals in high-quality territories reaching this developmental landmark faster than those in marginal habitats. The onset of reproductive maturity at this body size allows females to begin producing their first clutches while still maintaining the potential for further somatic growth.

Reproductive output in Anolis gundlachi has been assessed through long-term field observations of marked individuals. Under typical thermal conditions averaging 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females are capable of producing a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a characteristic common among anoline lizards. The frequency of these reproductive events is notable, with gravid individuals observed depositing eggs approximately every two to three weeks during the active breeding season. Based on a breeding period extending over roughly eight months of the year, this translates into an estimated 2.25 clutches per month [F_R_i = estimated 2.25 clutches per month] during that window, yielding approximately 18 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 18 eggs per year]. This sustained laying schedule places considerable energetic demand on females, who must forage actively to offset the caloric investment in yolk production and oviposition.

Longevity and the timing of first reproduction are significant components of the species' life history strategy. At a thermal regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum lifespan for Anolis gundlachi is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years], a relatively modest duration compared to larger anoles. The age at which a female attains a snout-vent length of 5 cm [Li = 5 cm], considered the ultimate adult size, is associated with an estimated wet weight of around 2.90 grams [Wwi = around 2.90 grams]. This adult body mass of 2.90 grams is modest compared to larger anoles such as A. cuvieri, consistent with the species' montane distribution and insectivorous diet. Reaching this asymptotic size marks the transition from a growing adult to a fully mature individual capable of maximum reproductive investment. The age at which individuals initiate their first reproduction in the wild corresponds to approximately 312 days after hatching [tR = approximately 312 days after hatching], with this value calculated from emergence, reflecting the time needed to complete somatic growth and secure a breeding territory at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C].
